title: How Cardinals Eat, Sleep & Vote While Locked In to Choose a Pope
asof: Rules from Universi Dominici Gregis (1996) · details from the May 2025 conclave · sources in description

shots.s: A hundred and thirty-three men walk into a chapel.
The doors close behind them.
No phones. No news. No TV.
They can't leave until they agree on one name.
And the world is watching a chimney.
So how do you eat,
sleep,
and vote,
locked inside the Vatican?
When a pope dies, cardinals choose the next one.
But only cardinals under eighty can vote.
In 2025, that was a hundred and thirty-three men.
They came from all over the world.
The rules come from a 1996 document by Pope John Paul the Second.
Its name is Universi Dominici Gregis.
Cardinals used to sleep on cots in small, stuffy rooms next to the Sistine Chapel.
Since 1996, there's a guesthouse inside the Vatican: Casa Santa Marta.
It was built with a conclave in mind.
It has a hundred and thirty-one rooms.
But Pope Francis lived there, and his rooms were sealed when he died.
That left about a hundred and twenty-five rooms, for a hundred and thirty-three cardinals.
So some stayed in the old building next door.
Who gets which room?
They draw lots.
Even when there's room for everyone.
Each bedroom has a bed, a dresser, a night table,
and a private bathroom with a shower.
It's comfortable, but it's not a luxury hotel.
The rooms have telephones.
But no cardinal may call anyone outside.
The internet is disconnected.
So is the satellite TV.
The rules forbid newspapers, radio and television for the whole election.
Every room is swept for hidden bugs and transmitters.
So is the Sistine Chapel.
The staff swear an oath of secrecy too.
Cooks, cleaners, doctors, even the elevator operators.
Break it, and the penalty is excommunication.
Casa Santa Marta has a dining room.
The rules say staff must be ready to cook and serve meals.
The cardinals eat there,
between voting sessions.
Then a short bus ride to the chapel.
On sealed, monitored buses.
Some cardinals in past conclaves insisted on walking instead, under watch.
The cardinals walk into the Sistine Chapel.
Each one swears an oath.
Then the order: "Extra omnes." Everybody out.
The doors close.
Each cardinal writes a name on a paper ballot.
The top says, in Latin: I elect as Supreme Pontiff.
They're told to disguise their handwriting.
Fold it twice, then walk it up to the altar.
To win, a candidate needs two thirds of the votes.
Two votes in the morning. Two in the afternoon.
After the votes, the ballots are burned in a stove.
The smoke goes up a chimney on the chapel roof.
Black smoke means no pope yet.
Crowds wait outside in Saint Peter's Square.
On the first night, the smoke was black.
The next afternoon, on the fourth vote,
the smoke was white.
The bells rang.
Cardinal Robert Prevost of the United States was the new pope.
He took the name Leo the Fourteenth.
The first pope from the United States.
Under the rules, what was said inside stays secret, forever.
Could you stay locked in until everyone agreed?
